The author studies an Einstein-frame gravity-plus-form action, using positivity rather than the flux equations of motion or Bianchi identities. A separate DBI stress-tensor calculation tests whether the same obstruction survives a particular nonlinear gauge-field action.

A weighted combination of radial and temporal Ricci components is expressed as an internal total derivative. Its integrated vanishing is combined with positive flux bilinears from Einstein's equation; the mixed Einstein equation then constrains the relative warp factors.

Estimate the second-vacuum strong scale using one-loop gauge-coupling running matched to the physical vacuum at the physical SUSY-breaking scale MS. The coefficients quoted are −7 for the SM and −3 for the MSSM; the proposed vacuum-energy estimate is Λ approximately ΛSQCD^4.

Analyze the stated positive-definite hidden-sector scalar potential through zeros of the hidden superpotential derivative. Compare the superpotential and supersymmetry realization at its degenerate minima; optional higher-order terms enlarge the possible vacuum set.

Solution generation uses lifting to a uniform black string, two boosts and T-duality, followed by KK reduction. At order α′, the authors use corrected T-duality rules in a Gauss-Bonnet scheme related to the string scheme by field redefinitions.

The Euclidean calculation uses surface gravity to fix the thermal period and boost/T-duality invariance of the action integrand to obtain the free energy. Mass and entropy follow from thermodynamic identities including charge chemical potentials.

A second entropy calculation uses Wald's Noether-charge formula, varying explicit curvature terms with respect to the Riemann tensor. The calculation is performed before KK reduction, using entropy invariance under that reduction.

Replace the continuum retarded Green function, supported on the future light cone up to normalization, by a link indicator. The field at a detector element counts linked source elements, multiplied by a charge prefactor; the detector signal sums this field over its active elements.

Compute the expected detector response and its leading correction in powers of the Planck length. The reported first correction is a boundary integral over the source region; fluctuation estimates are discussed more provisionally than the mean response.

The kinematical review uses longest-chain length for timelike distance and ordering-fraction or coarse-graining estimators for dimension. These translate order data into geometry only when a suitable manifold approximation exists.

Use signs of anomaly coefficients to classify factors as type 0, N or P and constrain shared matter. For growing classical rank, use large-rank trace coefficients to restrict representations. Appendix A uses explicit generators, traces and Young-diagram state counting to establish the type-0 positivity ingredient.

Prove finiteness by contradiction. A fixed gauge group admits only finitely many matter choices under the dimension-weighted gravitational anomaly condition. An infinite family must therefore have either unboundedly many bounded simple factors or a simple classical factor of unbounded rank.

Factorize the anomaly eight-form as I=(trR²−Σαi trFi²)(trR²−Σα̃i trFi²), after normalizing the coefficient of (trR²)² to one. Removal of irreducible terms requires nh−nv=244 and BAdj=ΣxRBR; additional equations determine real αi and α̃i.

Expands the quadratic quantum-field action as S0 + S1 + S2, where subscripts count background-scalar powers. Wick contractions of scalar and graviton propagators give the quadratic contribution ΓG = ⟨S2⟩ − ½⟨S1²⟩.

Uses the imported Vilkovisky–DeWitt construction, replacing the ordinary action Hessian by S,ij − Γ̄kij S,k. In Landau–DeWitt gauge, the required connection can be represented by the Christoffel connection of the specified field-space metric.
Extracts poles using dimensional regularization as n approaches four. FORM and Cadabra were used for some lengthy symbolic manipulations; this record does not reproduce those manipulations.

Rewrites the homogeneous equations as autonomous systems using Hubble-normalized field velocities and potential variables. Critical points are classified through existence conditions and Jacobian eigenvalues.
Uses effective exponents defined by 1/λeff² = 1/λ² + 1/µ² + a/(µλ) for the assisted potential, and 1/µeff² = (1−a²/4)/(λ²+µ²−aλµ) for the soft potential. These organize the fixed-point conditions.
Numerical integrations investigate trajectories between matter and scalar domination. A constant-a field redefinition diagonalizes the kinetic terms and is used to interpret the behavior near a = 2.

Diagnose supersymmetry through dilatino and gravitino variations and complex-type decomposition of G3. Estimate the four-dimensional gravitino mass by dimensional reduction of the ten-dimensional gravitino action.

Use the radial Green’s function to motivate source behavior, then integrate the sourced Einstein equation to match localized tension. Match charge through the constant part of the five-form function ℓ.

Solve linearized second-order supergravity equations directly, using power series around radial τ=0. Even and odd powers in the warp-factor perturbation decouple; singular source candidates are sought in the odd sector containing τ⁻¹.

Matches the thermal rate to a Bose-distribution integral of the polarization-averaged single-photon absorption rate. Comparing temperature-power coefficients determines its energy expansion, which the authors resum into the square of a modified Bessel function.

Places the bounce on a Euclidean-time cylinder of period β = 1/T and includes dynamical photons. Equivalently, photon exchange couples periodically repeated circular currents. Solving for their electromagnetic field gives the thermal correction to the action per period.

Uses the imported Euclidean bounce description with effective particle action S = mL − eEA. Its circular extremum has radius R = m/(eE) and action SB = πm²/(eE); a path integral around the bounce supplies the rate prefactor.

Construct local intrinsic-curvature counterterms. Use Hamilton–Jacobi counterterm results for the Gauss–Bonnet sector and asymptotic field redefinitions to rescale the two-derivative counterterms for the other sectors.

Obtain temperature from horizon regularity, entropy from Wald’s formula, energy from the boundary stress tensor and grand potential from the on-shell action. Impose T=0 together with the horizon equation to extract extremal mass/charge ratios.

Reduce perturbative order by substituting the lowest-order Einstein equation into higher-derivative variations. Separate the Gauss–Bonnet combination from the remaining curvature terms, then construct boundary terms cancelling normal derivatives of metric variations to O(αi).

Adapt the D3-dependent instanton superpotential to magnetized D7-branes by treating their induced D3 charge as a smeared source. Its backreaction on the warp factor and C4 changes the instanton action; expand the resulting functional around a holomorphic embedding.

Interpret the correction through a holomorphic Poisson β-deformation of complex geometry, derive Abelian F-flatness conditions, and use non-Abelian Seiberg–Witten maps, Moyal products, and locally commuting holomorphic frames to compare superpotentials off shell.

Component Noether calculations, current improvement terms, and embedding of improved R-currents, supercurrents and stress tensors into constrained real superfields. Compensated currents are calculated before freezing compensators and taking the decoupling limit.

The previously known chiral–linear duality is implemented through an intermediate Lagrangian: eliminating different fields yields the two descriptions. The authors identify this procedure as a superfield Legendre transformation.

Superfield constraint analysis, dimensional analysis and Lorentz symmetry restrict candidate FI contributions; repeated SUSY variations test component ansätze. The chiral argument tests whether additional conservation constraints follow from the original equations of motion.

The review uses homotopy classification of defects and Nambu–Goto worldsheet dynamics. Temporal/conformal gauge gives left- and right-moving waves in Minkowski space; expansion requires a different treatment and induces interactions between these modes.

Analytical network models and numerical simulations are reviewed, including interacting Abelian/non-Abelian field-theory analogues of bound-string networks and junction kinematics from Nambu–Goto equations supplemented by flux conservation.

Numerically solve coupled background, linear-growth and top-hat equations. Obtain matter spectra with CAMB using historical WMAP5 parameters apart from w. Estimate abundance with Press–Schechter ratios multiplying a smooth-quintessence Sheth–Tormen mass function.

Use spherical Fermi coordinates with metric departures from Minkowski suppressed by H²r². The local equations retain pressure as a gravitational source, ∇²Φ = 4πG(ρ + 3p), and combine Einstein equations with fluid continuity and Euler equations.

Expand the scalar as φ(t,x) = φ̄(t + π), derive its perturbation action and distinguish perturbations on scalar-field/velocity-orthogonal slices. The nonlinear-density application relies on the effective theory remaining valid despite large density contrast.

At V=0, write the potential as an exponential prefactor times a quadratic polynomial in x=(ReS,ReT,ImS,ImT). Analytically eliminate these fields using x0=−M⁻¹m, leaving the reduced function V_red=m0−mᵀM⁻¹m and equations V_red=∂ReZ V_red=∂ImZ V_red=0.

Apply the imported IIB/IIA dictionary to separate the potential into generalized NS-NS flux, R-R flux and two localized-source contributions. The IIA description includes H3, metric ω, Q and R fluxes, and even-degree R-R fluxes.

Use scaling and discrete transformations to scan θε∈[0,π]. Solve the Minkowski equation quadratically in tan θξ, numerically solve the remaining two equations for Z, and reconstruct S and T analytically. The reduced potential detects some instabilities, rather than replacing the complete stability analysis.

Reduce torus modular invariance to the finite matrix equations SNS† = TNT† = N, imposing entrywise nonnegative integer multiplicities and N11=1. The affine sl(2) proof described first finds invariant sesquilinear forms without positivity and then selects the admissible coefficients.

Compare the two annulus evolution channels using Cardy's equation; use the Verlinde formula to relate modular S to fusion coefficients. Boundary multiplicity matrices then supply nonnegative integer matrix representations of the fusion algebra, enabling a graph spectral classification.
Use ADM mass, entropy, the Smarr relation and the first law to compute CQ=T(∂S/∂T)Q. Its numerator is positive and its sign is controlled by the denominator (5−p)sinh²θ−1.
Compare Helmholtz free energies per unit brane volume, F=(M−TS)/Vp, using the reduced quantity F̄=(7−p)gsF/(2Q). The comparison is exact for D4 and asymptotic for p<4 when C≪Cmax.

Eliminate r0 between charge and temperature to obtain QT^(7−p)=Ap C(θ), where Ap=Ω8−p(7−p)^(8−p)/[2κ²gs(4π)^(7−p)] and C(θ)=sinhθ/cosh^(6−p)θ. Extrema and limiting behavior of this function organize the branches.

Solve Green-Schwarz factorization with real αi, α̃i, vanishing irreducible trFi⁴ anomalies and nh−nv=244. Blocks are joined using αiα̃j+αjα̃i=4ΣxijRS AiR AjS; shared matter prevents naïve addition of block gravitational-anomaly contributions.

Construct explicit examples with Weierstrass coefficients f,g in −4K,−6K and discriminant Δ=4f³+27g². Tune vanishing orders and impose split conditions from Tate’s algorithm; count remaining polynomial coefficients and compare them with neutral hypermultiplets.

For SU(N) blocks with fundamental and two-index antisymmetric matter, use f=2N−a(N−8) and (α,α̃)=(2,a−2), up to exchange. Recursively combine compatible blocks, using the lower bound (nh−nv)i≥7Na/2+1 and adding neutral hypermultiplets to saturate the gravitational anomaly.

Rewrite background dynamics as an autonomous system using x1=φ̇/(√6H), x2=exp(−λφ/2)/(√3H), N=ln a and Y=X exp(λφ); discuss fixed points and their linear stability, specializing the stability discussion to d=1.

Expand scalar fluctuations to quadratic order and inspect their Hamiltonian coefficients. The UV discussion uses a Minkowski background and distinguishes classical sound-speed stability from quantum ghost stability.
Impose ρD=ρΛ, use the Friedmann and dark-energy conservation equations to obtain ΩD(z) and wD(z), and reconstruct X and the scalar trajectory by numerical integration.

Construct gauge-invariant black-hole perturbation equations, transform them to Schrödinger form, and inspect leading large-momentum potentials for superluminal quasinormal modes and negative wells associated with instabilities.

Solve the sound-channel equation in a small-momentum expansion with infalling horizon and Dirichlet boundary conditions. Match its dispersion relation to conformal hydrodynamics; determine the relaxation-time contribution numerically.
Extract CT from the on-shell quadratic graviton action, and compute energy-flux coefficients using a graviton insertion interacting with an AdS shockwave through the cubic action.

Discuss inter-vacuum transitions through Euclidean-action/WKB paths. For the Case III exit estimate, approximate the potential by a triangle, use ΓCD=M⁴exp(−SE) with M² approximated by false-vacuum V″, and compare Γ/H⁴ with the critical value 9/(4π).

Compare analytic slow-roll trajectories with numerical background evolution and integrate coupled adiabatic/entropy perturbations. Initial perturbations use the Bunch-Davies vacuum at k≫aH; their evolution couples after horizon exit.

Expand matrices in mutually commuting irreducible SU(2) blocks and canonically rescale their coefficients. Classify block sizes by unordered positive-integer partitions ΣαNα=N; exchanging blocks does not produce a new theory. The two-block count is floor(N/2), and higher counts are treated recursively.

Use motion in the inverted potential −V1 and an imported thin-wall kick Δχ′≈−nσ0 e^(−nχ*/2Mχ)/(2Mχ). A returning profile requires the kick magnitude to match twice the rolling speed at some χ*. Comparing at the barrier top gives a convenient sufficient test; asymptotic falloffs provide a separate test.

Numerically relax candidate walls using artificial friction, then evolve without friction. Construct thin-wall bubble initial data from relaxed planar profiles. Model identical-bubble collisions in hyperbolic coordinates using reflective boundaries and vary their initial separation.

Solve the Casimir-modified Friedmann equation and express conformal time through elliptic integrals. The future conformal extent is τ∞(α)=K(√[(1+α²)/(1+2α²)])/√(1+2α²). Compare this height with a width estimated from the maximal injectivity radius.

Complexify the time and curvature scale to obtain an asymptotically hyperbolic Euclidean geometry. Compute the critical BPS brane action from positive area minus a volume contribution, then test its unique minimum numerically. Positivity is assessed after normalization by 2π²ΘL³.

Construct supercurrents by coupling to an off-shell supergravity formulation, varying with respect to the gravitational prepotential and taking the flat-superspace limit. Compare old-minimal and new-minimal compensators and their different conservation equations.

Set the photino to zero, solve the algebraic auxiliary-D equation and substitute back into the component Lagrangian. Inspect the vacuum photino transformations to identify broken generators and an unbroken linear combination.

Use a constrained chiral scalar X with X+(g²/16)X D̄²X̄=W² to encode the hidden supersymmetry. Embed FI couplings into frozen background chiral superfields to construct duality-covariant deformations; interpret a nonzero auxiliary expectation value as the mechanism producing a photino Goldstino.

Three ultraviolet-completion routes are outlined: F-theory constructions, brane polarization, and a gravitating charged Fermi gas. D0-brane and simple product-cycle Dp examples yield z=2; moduli stabilization is assessed in restricted examples.

Nonlinear probe DBI dynamics, radially conserved charge/current fluxes, and reality conditions determine DC transport. Linearized gauge fluctuations with ingoing horizon conditions determine retarded optical response.

Massive-carrier calculations use Nambu–Goto drag, WKB and Bessel/Hankel matching, and Maxwell fluctuations on numerically determined brane embeddings. Illustrative numerics choose f=1−(v/v+)^(2+z), V(θ)=cosθ, and n=2.

Estimate instanton amplitudes through Λ⁴ proportional to e^(−SED1), and assess decay-constant hierarchies using cycle geometry and warping. Compare induced D3 charge and NS5 worldvolume KK masses parametrically with the single-axion monodromy construction.

Orthogonally rotate to longitudinal θ̃ and transverse r̃ coordinates, with sin ξ=fr/√(fr²+fθ²). Solve ∂r̃V=0 adiabatically and linearize around a trench minimum in the stated hierarchy regime. The effective inflaton is φeff=θ̃, with canonical kinetic term at leading order.
Numerically determine potential minima and solve all retained background field equations, then transform to approximately canonical fields and calculate perturbation spectra and tilts at Hubble exit.

Project perturbations parallel and orthogonal to the background trajectory, construct curvature/entropy covariance spectra, and use a transfer-matrix formalism to describe possible superhorizon entropy-to-curvature conversion.

In spatially flat gauge, set u=aδφ, diagonalize the perturbation matrix M, and express modes through Hankel functions with μ_I²=9/4+3λ_I. Minkowski-like subhorizon vacuum conditions select the solution; heavy modes use large imaginary-order asymptotics.

Apply the imported closed-time-path prescription with Euclidean caps and forward/backward Lorentzian segments. With outward normals, matching requires Lh=Eh and LK=−i EK, together with a corner-normal condition. Scalar correlators follow from a Schottky image sum, Weyl transformation and suitable analytic continuation.

Uniformize S as H/Γ with nonidentity elements hyperbolic, |tr γ|>2, and extend Γ diagonally into the AdS3 isometry group. On the universal cover, remove points causally related to the boundary limit set before quotienting to avoid closed causal curves.

Use the terminating three-dimensional Fefferman–Graham expansion and holographic stress tensor. A locally biholomorphic uniformization map J specifies the handlebody filling through J∘γd=J for bulk-contractible cycles; its Schwarzian enters the boundary stress tensor.

Expand the potential to cubic order near the inflection point, characterize its slope and cubic derivative by λ1 and λ3, and use slow-roll e-fold integrals and scalar perturbation formulas. Numerical evolution uses the full noncanonical inflaton equation with σ(0)=σ1 and σ′(0)=0.

Derive the magnetic-flux correction to the D7 gauge kinetic function from the DBI expansion and express fΣ through flux coefficients and intersection data. Compute modulus and anomaly soft terms, using α to measure their relative importance and modular weights to parameterize matter metrics.

Expand the supergravity potential at large volume; compute moduli F-terms and matter-metric sectional curvatures; insert them into the supergravity soft-mass formula. The universal-mass calculation retains F^s contributions and subleading curvature terms important for its sign.

Apply the imported Kaplunovsky–Louis physical gauge-coupling formalism, including anomalous frame and canonical-normalization transformations, and extract its F-component. Estimate scalar masses through one-loop gauge-dominated RG evolution using the invariance of M_i/g_i².

Construct alternative regulators from linear combinations of finite translation operators, compare their small-β Taylor coefficients, and study zeros of f′ in the resulting classical Hamilton equations. An infinite sine-series example is used to challenge generic singularity resolution.

Retain the vanishing Hamiltonian constraint rather than merely the conserved energy of the gauge-fixed Lagrangian. Factor the constraint and compute ratios of Hamiltonian flows to obtain the gauge-invariant evolution dv/dφ.

Legendre-transform the modified Hamiltonian explicitly for f=sin. Relate the resulting expansion in powers of ȧ/a to curvature invariants using traces R(n) of Ricci-tensor powers, integration by parts and an appendix induction in conformal time.

Use the pole/residue expansion of tree-level Veneziano-type scattering amplitudes as a qualitative analogy: factorial factors suppress couplings to highly excited states despite exponential level degeneracy. This scattering discussion motivates, rather than directly computes, black-hole emission.

Represent closed-string emission by an effective black-hole vertex. For k=l+r oscillators, the assumed vertex contains k momenta and M_10^−(k+2), giving Γ_single∼T(T/M_10)^(2k+4). Count states at fixed oscillator number using integer partitions before summing accessible levels.

Model Hawking energy loss as dM_BH/dt≈−T²N_eff, with species weighted by Boltzmann suppression and the overlap of their extra-dimensional wavefunctions with the horizon. Compare KK counting with dimensional-reduction relations.

Exploit factorization of Kähler and complex-structure sectors to construct directional derivative inequalities for V. Positive semidefinite contributions to the potential-gradient norm can be discarded to obtain lower bounds on ε.

Expand fields and fluxes in finite, orientifold-parity-selected left-invariant forms, allowing nonclosure. Obtain K and W from generalized-structure expressions and evaluate the N=1 F-term potential V=eᴷ(K^{M N̄}D_MW D_N̄W̄−3|W|²). Supersymmetric vacua are studied through F-term equations.
Identify formal T-dual Kähler and superpotentials in IIA; generic duals require nongeometric Q-flux. Search the SU(2) × SU(2) potential numerically using Mathematica and STRINGVACUA.

Use the imported Borokhov-Gubser formalism: a one-dimensional superpotential permits eight linearized second-order equations to be written as sixteen first-order equations, with the eight conjugate ξ equations forming a closed subsystem. The ξ variables measure departures from supersymmetric gradient flow.

Solve by homogeneous solutions and variation of parameters, obtaining integral expressions and separate infrared and ultraviolet series. UV/IR constants generally differ by additive shifts; the X₁ constants are instead multiplicatively related. Full integral expressions allow numerical matching in principle.

Combine boundary-condition matching with DBI/Wess-Zumino probe-force cancellations. Calibrate the perturbation framework against BPS D3-branes, whose charge shift produces the expected smeared-source 1/τ warp-factor singularity.

Numerical integration evolves the background and up to three mode functions for arbitrary momentum triangles. Early subhorizon integrals use partial integration and approximate Bunch–Davies modes; subsequent evolution uses full numerical modes, typically beginning 4–6 e-folds inside the horizon.

ADM perturbation theory in the gauge with no inflaton fluctuations; quantization of ζ in the Bunch–Davies vacuum; cubic interaction Hamiltonian and in-in integration, including the field redefinition accounting for neglected boundary terms.

Estimate Stückelberg masses through a simplified 2×2 mass-squared matrix contrasting small-cycle and large-cycle U(1)s. Distinguish contributions from two orientifold-parity classes of axions and their volume scalings.

Use holomorphic gauge-kinetic mixing and a Kaplunovsky-Louis-type relation to pass to physical gauge couplings and kinetic mixing. Separate perturbative complex-structure/brane-position dependence from nonperturbative Kähler-modulus dependence.

Analyze a hidden Higgs pair with soft masses and a D-term potential. Kinetic mixing induces a hidden Fayet-Iliopoulos term from the visible hypercharge D-term. An additional Stückelberg-massive U(1) is considered to alter the Higgs quartic and separate gauge-boson and Higgs masses.

Extract the effective metric from the quadratic fluctuation kinetic operator and analyze its characteristic cone. Weak static vacuum backgrounds satisfy Laplace's equation; a local Taylor expansion yields a traceless spatial Hessian controlling the cone shift.

Construct conformal interactions from curvature invariants of the fictitious metric. Compute stress energy by metric variation and its trace; homogeneity, scale invariance, and conservation imply zero background energy density, leaving pressure to determine NEC violation.

Use forward dispersion relations with the optical theorem to constrain the EFT cutoff, and fixed-positive-t dispersion relations to test non-forward amplitude positivity. The latter analysis isolates the tree-level order-s³ amplitude.

Structure constants in two SO(3,3) factors are organized into four symmetric SL(4) charge matrices. Jacobi identities constrain their allowed combinations; in the restricted (semi-)simple cases the paired matrices are proportional. Dilatonic potentials are expressed through a superpotential. This also exposes a one-parameter family of SO(3,1) embeddings, including a null embedding.

The authors construct parity-invariant gauge tensors, truncate by Z2, and analyze the resulting potential and scalar mass matrix to determine whether tachyons survive. Some gauge couplings must be set to zero for consistency; the listed singular limits are stated to preserve the de Sitter extremum.

The extragalactic photon calculation integrates evolving PBH emission over cosmic time with redshift and propagation limits. Abundance caps touch upper 1σ observational error tips; known astrophysical contributions are not subtracted.
PYTHIA Monte Carlo fragmentation supplies injected hadron and photon energy spectra, including photons from unstable hadrons and fragmentation bremsstrahlung.
Coupled Boltzmann equations add neutron/proton interconversion, hadronic showers and photodissociation to standard BBN, followed with KAWANO 4.1 and updated nuclear cross sections.

At order λ^2, invariant position-space integrals of G^4 determine the vacuum effective action. Analytic continuation in dimension and complex-plane sum rules isolate the obstruction to Wick rotation and its dimensional parity.

A finite-time S-matrix identity yields kinetic collision terms with N for destroyed particles and 1+N for created bosons. Large-momentum logarithms become secular time dependence through pmax=Λe^T; the kinetic treatment resums leading (λ^2T)^n terms.

Legendre/Gegenbauer mode-overlap integrals and contour deformation test vacuum-to-four-particle production and one-to-three-particle decay. Branch points and angular-momentum selection rules control cancellations.

Scalar spectra are extracted from the four-dimensional potential of the consistent left-invariant N=2 truncation. The authors use N=1 superpotential and Kähler-potential technology for the retained scalars, accounting separately for the additional axion omitted by that description.

Expand internal RR fluxes in J, normalized W2, their wedge products, and the volume form, with H proportional to ReΩ. Substitution into the ten-dimensional Bianchi identities, flux equations, dilaton equation, and Einstein equations produces algebraic equations for seven flux coefficients, solved numerically for the shape-dependent families.

Compute Yukawas through internal wave-function overlaps. Sum Kaluza-Klein threshold effects using Laplacian determinants, expressed through holomorphic Ray-Singer torsion with zeta-function regularization and zero modes omitted.

Identify massless matter with Dirac zero modes on curves. For abelian backgrounds, index theory gives net chirality through charge-weighted integrals of F/(2π); this counts the chiral index rather than the complete vector-like spectrum.

Use eight-dimensional gauge theory and position-dependent adjoint Higgs fields to describe singularity unfolding and matter localization. Casimirs encode geometric deformations; the supersymmetric fields organize as W(0,0), A(0,1), and Φ(2,0) on S.

Use supersymmetric background fields, dimensional reduction, and composite-operator mixing to recover the anomalous-dimension contribution. The manifestly supersymmetric calculation evaluates the matter-background contribution to the expectation value of W².

Compute Green's functions with insertions obtained by supersymmetry variation of the supersymmetry-current gamma trace. Interpret their contact terms as transformations of external fields and use them to identify the mixed current.

Compare rescaling Jacobians at two ultraviolet cutoffs using the same rescaling factor. Their difference isolates the contribution of a finite momentum shell, separating renormalizable terms from cutoff-suppressed operators.

Translate fluxes into embedding-tensor components and impose the N=4 quadratic constraints. The first constraint expresses closure/Jacobi consistency; the second expresses charge orthogonality and supplies relations among the redundant electric and magnetic generators.

For the two-factor comparison, use SO(3,3)≃SL(4) and two symmetric matrices M and M̃ to parameterize structure constants. The stated Jacobi condition requires M M̃ to be proportional to the identity; in the diagonal presentation all four paired diagonal products are equal.

Trace-reverse the higher-dimensional Einstein equations and separately trace external and internal components. Evaluate these combinations for form-field and localized-source stress tensors to obtain a pointwise internal-curvature inequality.

For warped metrics, combine the internal trace with the warp-factor constraint, integrate against u^α, and integrate by parts. Choosing α=2/d removes the explicit warp-gradient term in the resulting weighted identity.

Analyze conformal transformations through v=e^(2B), the integrated scalar-curvature functional, and fixed-volume Yamabe minimization. Assess finite-field effective potentials through a Kaluza-Klein expansion around a higher-dimensional near-solution.

ADM decomposition and variation with respect to the spatial metric and projectable lapse produce the FRW evolution equation and global lapse constraint. Assuming standard matter conservation, the evolution equation is integrated to obtain a first Friedmann equation with C/a³.

Auxiliary fields A and B linearize the action in R̃: variation gives A=R̃ and B=F′(A). Canonical momenta, constraint preservation, Poisson brackets and reduction by Dirac brackets are then used for the Hamiltonian analysis.
Constant-H vacuum solutions reduce the FRW equations to an algebraic condition on F and F′. Quadratic and cubic polynomial choices of F are examined for nonzero de Sitter roots.

Inside and outside a constant-density sphere, the effective potential is approximated quadratically around the appropriate minimum. Solutions obey φ′(0)=0 and φ(∞)=φ₀, with φ and its first derivative matched at the surface.
For pressureless spherical sources, the radial equation is φ″+2φ′/r=V,φ+ρA,φ. Approximately homogeneous regions are described by Veff=V+ρA.

Construct pure-gauge SU(2) connections by parallelizing an orthonormal isotriplet, classify them using a Chern–Simons winding number, and build vielbein triples from left-invariant one-forms. Transform to temporal gauge to compare vacuum endpoints.

Use radial vielbein and contortion ansätze built with ’t Hooft matrices. The Eguchi–Hanson analysis combines asymptotic gauge transformations with numerical gauge-function solutions; contortion self-duality reduces selected ansätze to ordinary differential equations.
AdS/CFT operator matching and supersymmetry-breaking spurions organize the field-theory interpretation. D7 gaugino-bilinear couplings are varied as localized sources for the bulk flux equation.

A Green's-function solution separates the flux-sourced potential from arbitrary harmonic contributions. Four-dimensional curvature is included through a modified-Bessel solution and an iterative Green's-function expansion.
Closed IASD three-forms are built from the Kähler form J, holomorphic three-form Ω and scalar harmonic functions. Angular harmonic analysis determines radial exponents and the dual operator spectrum.

The action is reduced using integration by parts with surface terms discarded, commutator and Bianchi identities, and the vanishing three-dimensional Weyl tensor. Excitations are studied by gauge-fixed perturbation theory about flat spacetime.

Weighted engineering dimensions use [dx]=[κ]^-1 and [dt]=[κ]^-z. The leading gravitational kinetic and spatial couplings have dimension [κ]^(d−z); choosing z=d makes them dimensionless. A polynomial Lifshitz scalar provides the pedagogical comparison.

Use leading-order in-in perturbation theory with the dominant interaction HI⊃−∫d³x a³εδ̇R²Ṙ. Unperturbed mode functions suffice at the retained order; the authors estimate derivative corrections during resonance to justify this approximation.

Expand the background and Mukhanov–Sasaki mode equation to first order in modulation strength. Hankel-mode mixing is expressed using incomplete Gamma functions; stationary phase isolates the resonant contribution and its late-time amplitude.

Compare primordial shapes through the normalized scalar product built from F(S,S′)=∫dk1dk2dk3 SS′/K. Numerical and semi-analytical evaluations retain a three-dimensional momentum domain with finite-range infrared and ultraviolet regulation.

Review and apply Gulotta's inverse dimer algorithm: embed a rotated toric diagram in a rectangular conifold orbifold, then partially resolve it by merging zigzag paths in Farey-tree order. Consistency requires controlling additional crossings and preserving the winding/web correspondence.

Extract Higgs-dependent Yukawa matrices from superpotentials, diagonalize YY† to obtain left-handed rotations, and calculate CKM mixing. CP violation is characterized by the Jarlskog invariant and the commutator of the up- and down-sector Hermitian mass matrices.

Family counting examines local dimer operations, consistent additional crossings and toric-preserving Seiberg duality. Yukawa-rank arguments start from rectangular-grid perfect matchings and follow Higgsing plus integration of massive fields to daughter theories.

Analyze superspace conservation constraints, component expansions, and improvements by a real superfield U. Track whether improvements are local, gauge invariant, and globally defined, then use preservation of the FZ operator equation along RG flow.

Gauge current multiplets using a real gravitational superfield H, identify residual gauge symmetries and off-shell fields, and introduce compensators. Dualizing a real linear multiplet G to a chiral Φ exposes the additional propagating matter multiplet.

Reviewed Hamilton–Jacobi formulation: characteristic function S=2e^U W, with W²+2G^{rs}∂rW∂sW=V. The radial equations are U̇=e^U W and φ̇^r=2e^U G^{rs}∂sW. For the chosen solution class, W(φ0,P)=∫_{−∞}^0 e^{2U}V dτ=M_ADM; Appendix A derives the flow by varying boundary data.

Charge-stabilizer analysis uses adapted coset representatives L=L0L1, Cartan decompositions, Killing vectors and vielbeins; the I4<0 branch uses an Iwasawa/solvable parametrization. Small-orbit W functions are obtained through constrained I4→0 limits of known large-orbit functions expressed in H-invariants.

Review Witten's bubble by double Wick rotation of five-dimensional Schwarzschild geometry. Smooth closure of the circle fixes its coordinate periodicity, and the resulting tip contains a dS₃ bubble worldvolume and a cigar-shaped transverse disk.

Reduce the coupled Einstein–scalar equations to radial equations, determine exact asymptotic data, and integrate outward using a near-core expansion. For n=1 the shooting parameters are ℓ and the leading scalar slope f′₀; Euclidean actions are obtained by background subtraction.

Construct the four-dimensional Kähler potential and flux superpotential, extremize the scalar potential, and examine canonically normalized moduli/axion mass matrices against the BF bound. Blow-up effects are expanded in δ=√|eA³/(e1e2e3)|, retaining their leading stabilizing potential.

Use Coleman–De Luccia thin-wall bounces and compare the calibrated lower bound TL=2e^(K/2)|ΔW| with the gravitational ceiling. A finite AdS-to-AdS bounce requires T<√(4/3)(√|V−|−√|V+|); for a small energy difference this gives TU≈ε/√(3|V0|). Holomorphic wrapped cycles can saturate TL.

Metric variation and the trace equation 3□F+FR−2f=κ²T identify the scalaron. An auxiliary-field action establishes a scalar-tensor representation; a conformal transformation constructs the Einstein-frame action.

Background viability is analyzed through autonomous variables, an m(r) phase plane and fixed-point Jacobian eigenvalues. Perturbations use gauge-invariant variables and a quadratic action fixing the canonical normalization u=a√Qs ℛ; constant slow-roll parameters permit Hankel-function solutions.

Couple each supergravity prepotential to an external source, vary under linearized gauge transformations with unconstrained spinor parameter Lα, and demand invariance. This directly yields the supercurrent conservation law and compensator-source constraints.

Write quadratic actions with superspin projectors and use superspace D-algebra identities. Improvement transformations relate source multiplets, while superfield dualities exchange real linear compensators for chiral fields.

Use universal Einstein-frame scalings VH∼τ^−2ρ^−3, VFp∼τ^−4ρ^(3−p), VOq∼τ^−3ρ^((q−6)/2), and VR6∼τ^−2ρ^−1. Flux contributions are nonnegative, orientifold contributions nonpositive, and the curvature contribution has either sign.

Search for D=−aτ∂τ−bρ∂ρ satisfying DV≥cV with c>0, which excludes positive-energy stationary points and bounds slow roll. Refined tests use the split vol6=ρ(2)ρ(4)² and, in IIB, additional complex-structure directions; satisfying a universal test does not exhaust the scalar directions.

Compute soft terms through supergravity F-terms, the inverse Kähler metric, gauge kinetic functions and matter metrics. Treat redefinition in the moduli Kähler potential first, then include it in matter metrics and impose D-term stabilization of the visible cycle.

Insert re-expressed physical volumes into the Kähler potential, evaluate V=e^K(K^(i j̄)DiW D j̄W̄−3|W|²), and solve stationarity conditions using large-aτs and small-redefinition expansions. Compare approximate minima with numerical extrema for selected parameter values.

Initial conditions use Eddington inversion for an isotropic distribution function, an exponentially truncated NFW density profile chosen to preserve distribution-function positivity, and acceptance–rejection sampling of radii and speeds.

NFW parameters are fitted using χ² and Poisson likelihoods for radial particle counts. Interpolated mass and concentration changes map initial ΛCDM halos to decay halos; the cluster calculation transforms the imported Tinker differential mass function using the initial-to-final mass Jacobian.

Modified GADGET-2 runs in Newtonian, noncosmological mode. Each timestep samples decay with probability Δt/τ, maintaining Δtmax/τ≪1; a decayed particle receives one randomly directed kick and cannot decay again.

Shear viscosity is obtained from the low-frequency radial canonical momentum of a transverse metric fluctuation; entropy density uses Wald's formula. The appendix evaluates the resulting horizon expressions using the zeroth-order solution.

Thermodynamics uses background-subtracted black-hole and AdS actions, differentiation of the free energy, and the thermodynamic energy identity. These thermodynamic results are introduced as previously calculated in [4].

Holographic trace-anomaly results identify c1 with central charges. Imported bounds are a/c∈[1/3,31/18], [1/2,3/2], and [1/2,5/4] for N=0,1,2 respectively; their coupling restrictions are intersected with the proposed WGC restriction.

Thermal relic abundances are obtained numerically from dn/dt = −3Hn − ⟨σAv⟩(n²−neq²), with an approximate freeze-out criterion n⟨σAv⟩ = H. Chemical freeze-out is distinguished from kinetic decoupling.
Solar capture and annihilation are modeled by Ṅ = C−AN². In equilibrium ΓA ≈ C/2; converting neutrino limits into scattering limits additionally requires assumptions about annihilation products.

A tortoise-coordinate Klein–Gordon analysis motivates effectively massless radial propagation near a simple horizon. The authors then use a flat-space 1PI graviton propagator and Källén–Lehmann spectral positivity to argue for enhanced gravitational couplings.

Integrate the first law dS=β(M)dM and use β≥RS together with the asserted radius relation RS;X=M[1+IX(M)] in Planck units. Combine the resulting entropy estimate with an imported semiclassical evaporation bound.

Wald entropy is expressed using an effective coupling for r,t-polarized gravitons. For Lovelock branes, the analysis examines purely spatial Riemann components at the horizon and argues that their higher-curvature entropy contributions vanish.

For group manifolds, use left-invariant Maurer–Cartan forms, orientifold parity, Jacobi identities and a previously derived de Sitter no-go criterion to restrict candidate algebras. The authors then test torsion constraints on four candidate algebras.

Numerical solution branches are parameterized by f2/f1 after removing an overall scale. Stability of the explicit family is studied using an N=1 scalar potential and the 14×14 mass matrix for left-invariant fluctuations.

Express the Ricci tensor through torsion classes and decompose symmetric tensors into SU(3) singlet, 8, and 6+6̄ components. Insert the flux/source ansatz into Bianchi identities, flux equations, dilaton equation and Einstein equations to obtain geometric constraints and algebraic coefficient relations.
Reduce to a four-dimensional Einstein-frame potential for volume ρ and dilaton σ=ρ^(3/2)e^(−φ̃). Different volume scalings of X components generate additional source terms b1 and b2.
Expand an odd, generally nonpure polyform X− in the pure-spinor Hodge diamond and vary the resulting source action. Proposed equations d_H Re X−=0 and d_H Im X−=c0 gs ∗λ(F) organize the flux sector.

Construct invariant one-forms using the adjoint-action twist A_M=exp(−t ad∂t). Use the reviewed almost abelian lattice criterion: some nonzero t0 must make exp(t0 ad∂t) conjugate to an integer matrix.

Integrate out Stückelberg-massive anomalous vectors to identify residual infrared symmetries. Rotate the axion out of FN terms with a PQ transformation to obtain derivative matter couplings and gauge-anomaly interactions.
Estimate scales by matching FN-suppressed fermion masses and neutrino operators: φ²(h†l)²/M³ in A versus (h†l)²/M in B, together with light-fermion Yukawa operators containing one φ/M factor.

Expand fields in the globally defined structure forms η, J and Ω, whose algebra closes under exterior differentiation and Hodge duality. Substitution into ten-dimensional equations removes internal-coordinate dependence, providing the authors' consistency argument.

Implement F5 self-duality using Lagrange multipliers and auxiliary field strengths before eliminating redundant fields. The complex two-form obeys a first-order equation; its associated vector supplies gauge degrees of freedom eaten by the tensor.

Use a solvable parameterization to match the scalar coset metric and vector couplings to N=4 supergravity. Extract the embedding tensor from covariant derivatives: its components distinguish geometric flux from RR five-form flux.

Crossed-module algebra replaces categorical diagrams with groups and maps satisfying t(α(g)h)=gt(h)g⁻¹ and α(t(h))h′=hh′h⁻¹. A 2-morphism (g,h) goes from g to t(h)g; horizontal composition gives the semidirect product G⋉H.

Path groupoids use thin homotopy classes of lazy paths; the surface analogue uses lazy surfaces modulo thin homotopies. Thinness requires differential rank <2 for path homotopies and <3 for surface homotopies. Whiskering and the pasting theorem organize surface subdivision.
Count deformations through polynomial coefficients, adjunction, Riemann–Roch and Riemann–Hurwitz; compare normal-bundle counting with odd canonical sections on a smooth abstract double-cover curve.

Treat four-form flux as a linear map between the K3 cohomologies. The appendix relates the minimum condition to diagonalizability of G^aG with nonnegative eigenvalues, using bases with three positive and nineteen negative directions.

Construct cycles by fibering elliptic-fibre one-cycles over paths or real surfaces in the base; use periods and intersection matrices to identify brane displacement, recombination and gauge enhancement.

For SE5, identify the gauged generators from scalar covariant derivatives using the embedding-tensor framework. Analyze the scalar potential for AdS critical points and diagonalize fluctuations around the supersymmetric vacuum to extract masses.

Construct metric and form-strength ansätze from the globally defined SU(2)-structure forms J, Ω and η, imposing five-form self-duality in the ansatz. Substitute into the ten-dimensional Bianchi identities and equations of motion; the authors establish consistency by cancellation of internal-coordinate dependence.

For HK4 × S1, dualize the two real two-forms into vectors, redefine scalars, and use a solvable Lie algebra parametrization of SO(5,2)/(SO(5)×SO(2)). Match scalar, vector and Chern–Simons terms to the standard ungauged N=4 action.

Analyze normalizable radial modes in hard-wall AdS using Bessel functions and an illustrative Dirichlet IR condition. Large operator dimensions give heavier four-dimensional resonances; a semiclassical string falling to the IR wall supplies a complementary redshift argument.

Relate curvature, internal volume and degrees of freedom through dimensional reduction and the holographic conformal anomaly. Expand flavour-brane DBI actions to extract five-dimensional gauge couplings and the strong-sector contribution to SM running.

Use Wilson-loop ladder resummation, converted into a Schrödinger problem, to motivate the short-distance strong-coupling potential. Combine its extrapolated behaviour with the imported concavity result for static potentials to constrain the confining string tension.

Survival probabilities are computed by excluding nucleation events from the relevant past-light-cone region: P(C)=exp[-Γ Vol(C)]. The appendix evaluates this volume for observers and regulated boundary surfaces.

The imported CdL prescription uses an invariant Euclidean saddle as Lorentzian initial data. Hyperbolic interior/exterior coordinates and Israel junction conditions then match the two AdS geometries across a tensionful wall.
The analysis specializes the imported BKMU B-type construction: K=Σ_i c_i ln det_(η_i)(ξ†ξ), with ξ(φ')=gξ(φ)ĥ^-1. The holomorphic Kähler shift is F=Σ_i c_i ln det_(η_i)(ĥ^-1).

The proof analyzes projected traces using the simple, abelian and nilpotent parts of Ĥ. A complementary hidden-local-symmetry formulation introduces an auxiliary vector superfield, eliminates it algebraically and gauge-fixes the chiral fields to recover the nonlinear sigma model.

Steepest descent and numerical saddle solutions approximate the exact integral. Inclusion–exclusion counts states with exactly j occupied flux directions; numerical sampling and brute-force searches support selected approximations. Thin-shell counts use Nε≈ω_J(R0)Λε/R0.

The lattice count is differentiated into a Dirac-delta density, represented by a vertical contour integral, and factorized into Jacobi theta functions. Poisson summation supplies the theta functional equation and its complementary asymptotic limits.

Retain the singlet dependence of the potential, analyze Higgs and singlet phases, and test stability in both frames. Include the scalar-curvature contribution in the Jordan frame and canonical normalization in the Einstein frame; compare the singlet mass with H² and compute the transverse slow-roll parameter.

Start from the superconformal action and fix the extra local symmetries: bμ=0 for special conformal transformations, N=Φ for dilatations, y=ȳ for U(1), and χ0=0 for S-supersymmetry. Translate conformal fields to physical fields using modified Kähler-covariant derivatives.

Combines string/Planck scale relations, D-brane gravitational backreaction, black-hole/string entropy matching, and dimensional reduction to compare independently motivated species counts. These are scaling arguments with numerical factors suppressed.

A species-resolving detector pixel must contain samples of all N species or equivalent information. Localization costs at least N/L_pixel in energy; requiring its Schwarzschild radius to remain smaller than the pixel yields the species-resolution scale.

Defines effective N through black-hole emission normalized to the massless-graviton rate. Uses a semiclassicality parameter ξ≪1 and, in ten dimensions, ξ=(T/M_10)^8 N to constrain the temperature at which semiclassical evaporation fails.
Constructs CP1 through two charge-p chiral fields with K=|z1|²e^{pV}+|z2|²e^{pV}−ξV. Eliminating V gives K_eff=(ξ/p)log(1+|Φ|²) and f_π²=ξ/p; the global gauge group controls allowed wrapping numbers.

Uses Kähler transformation laws of the superpotential and fermions to identify FI gauge transformations as R-transformations. Compact gauge periodicity then imposes charge quantization; a separate expansion in ξ/M_P² recovers rigid-limit symmetry restrictions.

Adds a local BF-type coupling between a multiplier λ, instanton density ν, and a compact gauge field strength F. Gauge-field variation makes λ constant; multiplier variation imposes ν=pF/(2π), restricting integrated instanton number without adding propagating local fields.

Power counting tracks volume suppression in cubic, quartic and derivative interactions. Boson–fermion mass differences then estimate supersymmetry-breaking corrections, rather than treating each heavy state independently.

Dimensional regularization and RG threshold estimates establish scalar naturalness benchmarks. Higher-dimensional heavy fields are integrated out into local curvature invariants; the appendix relates higher-dimensional phase space to summing KK modes.

Evolves Ω_de using dΩ_de/dz=−Ω_de(1−Ω_de)[3/(1+z)−2√Ω_de/n], then obtains w_de=−1+2√Ω_de/(3na). These relations determine the scalar reconstruction once n and the matter-era initial condition are chosen.

For N identical fields, derives a per-field excursion suppressed by N^−1/2 and reconstructs V(ϕ)/ρ_c0=(1−w_de)Ω_de E²/(2N). Compares the excursion suppression with an imported conjectural N-dependent gravity-scale bound.

Reconstructs scalar excursion through a redshift integral with integrand √[3(1+w_de)Ω_de]/(1+z), choosing the present field value to vanish. Reported field-evolution plots are used to impose the proposed excursion threshold.

State–operator correspondence and OPE factorization organize CFT observables into sequence-space data. Heat evolution suppresses high-dimension contributions; sewing pairs of pants relates OPE norms to genus-two partition functions and spectral terms to genus-one amplitudes.

Whitney and Nash embedding results motivate possible QFT embedding statements. The geometric analogy seeks to reproduce sigma-model potentials, metrics and B-fields using constrained ambient fields; these analogies do not themselves establish a QFT embedding theorem.

Kibble–Turok left/right-moving solutions provide loop kinematics. Linearized Einstein equations, Fourier-transformed string stress energy and near-cusp Taylor expansions yield small-angle oscillatory integrals; geometric-optics substitutions introduce cosmological redshift and distance.

Codimension counting estimates near-cusp measures, supported by explicit low-harmonic loop families. Burst forecasts compare Damour–Vilenkin interpolating functions with direct numerical redshift integration using cosmological time and angular-diameter distance.

Reproduces an earlier species-resolution argument: comparing an unknown label with N sample species requires energy at least N/L in the measurement region. Requiring this region to exceed its gravitational radius yields the species length.

Massive-pole examples and a two-scalar gravitational toy model examine heavy-state exchange and long-distance corrections through second order in Newton's constant. Entropy and Hawking-Boltzmann arguments then motivate suppression after the proposed particle-to-black-hole transition.

Localization thought experiment: resolving L requires energy E ≳ 1/L within L. The authors compare L with the Schwarzschild radius R(L) ~ L_P²/L to argue that attempted sub-Planckian measurements instead form macroscopic black holes.
Evolve separate Fourier-space linear perturbations for galaxies and pressureless matter, then calculate galaxy growth, weak-lensing and ISW response parameters, and EG.
Construct a matter-density-dependent effective potential, locate its minimum, and estimate the mass and fifth-force coupling of perturbations around that minimum.

Derive necessary screening inequalities and numerically integrate the radial field equation for an NFW halo. Local tests use the paper-era Cassini long-range bound αlocal<1.2×10⁻⁵ for a range exceeding approximately 9–10 AU.

Superconformal tensor calculus combines rigid supersymmetry with local conformal invariance. A scalar compensator multiplet is gauge fixed to obtain the relevant bosonic curvature and S-dependent terms, without executing the complete fermionic conformal construction.

For the parity-preserving auxiliary-S theory, |μ| → ∞ removes the Lorentz Chern-Simons term, while the distinct parameter μ̌ may remain finite. An auxiliary symmetric tensor replaces K, while S is retained during expansion about supersymmetric AdS. Field redefinitions diagonalize the quadratic action into Einstein, Fierz-Pauli, Proca, and possible scalar sectors; AdS representation theory supplies mass bounds.

Covariant Abbott-Deser-Tekin energy: linearize gravitational equations about vacuum AdS, construct a conserved current using a background timelike Killing vector, and express its charge as an asymptotic surface integral. Background AdS has zero energy by construction.

Compute viscosity using the stress-tensor Kubo formula, the quadratic transverse-graviton effective action, conserved low-frequency radial momentum and infalling horizon conditions. Compute entropy density using Wald's Noether-charge formula, with horizon-binormal normalization εµν εµν=−2.

Solve the charged metric and Maxwell equations perturbatively through O(α′²). Integration constants keep the coordinate horizon at r0 and leave the charge unchanged; the asymptotic mass coefficient and effective cosmological constant receive corrections.
Illustrate the constraints with h(x)=−α/x−α1 x², x=T̃+T̃*, and f(s̃)=m³[(log s̃)²+k log s̃+k1 s̃]. A plotted two-real-field potential is used to support the claimed AdS minimum.

Insert the two-modulus ansatz into the Einstein-frame supergravity F-term potential. Impose the T-sector relation (14) and cancellation-motivated constraint (15), then extremize with respect to the real components s̃ and t̃. The paper discusses second derivatives for selected functions.

Expand W and K in observable chiral fields, choose a diagonal observable Kähler metric, canonically normalize, and apply standard supergravity expressions for scalar masses and trilinear and bilinear soft coefficients. Planck factors are restored for order-of-magnitude estimates.

Expand and canonically normalize the Kähler kinetic terms order by order in inverse volume. Derive the scalar potential with leading α′, nonperturbative and string-loop contributions, then integrate out the heavy moduli adiabatically.

Use slow-roll parameters and an e-fold integral, suppress the inflaton contribution relative to COBE normalization, and estimate curvaton fluctuations from a quantum-versus-classical crossover. Evolve their fractional amplitude on superhorizon scales.

Obtain modulus couplings from the D7 gauge kinetic function, calculate visible gauge-boson decay rates, and apply sudden thermalization and sudden decay approximations to reheating, isocurvature conversion and nongaussianity.

Use running gauge couplings, gaugino condensation and the symmetry-constrained Affleck–Dine–Seiberg superpotential to analyse hidden SU(Nc) theories with Nf = 0 or 0 < Nf < Nc−1; include supersymmetry-breaking scalar masses when discussing their low-energy spectra.

Expand moduli about their vacuum values and diagonalise M² = ½K⁻¹V″, normalising eigenvectors with the Kähler metric. Expand open-string kinetic and mass terms in these canonical mass eigenstates to obtain couplings, decay rates and branching ratios.

Four-dimensional N=1 BPS equations are compared with expansions of the ten-dimensional flow. The reviewed superpotential prescription is W=√8∫Ω∧(Ĥ+i dJ); for the chosen mirror half-flat truncation with flux it gives W=√8(e_iT^i+ε_aZ^a+μ^aG_a), with projective Z^0=1 in this expression.

Spinor bilinears translate gravitino and dilatino Killing equations into differential conditions on G2 forms ϕ and Φ. A 6+1 decomposition uses ϕ=α∧J+Ω− and Φ=α∧Ω++(1/2)J∧J, then identifies SU(3) intrinsic torsion and transverse flow.

Analyze retained-modulus Hessians, orientifold projections and anisotropic deformations. Estimate brane-antibrane stability using discrete Wilson lines and T-duality. Assess localization corrections through warp-factor and p-form equations, distinguishing their pointwise role from their contribution to the averaged potential.

Use a (2,2) gauged linear sigma model and Weierstrass fibration to encode stringy cosmic-brane backreaction and curvature shifts. T-duality relates complex-structure and Kähler fibrations. Gradient energy from fiber boundary conditions helps stabilize fiber size and the varying B-field component.

Dimensionally reduce the ten-dimensional string-frame action, Weyl-rescale to lower-dimensional Einstein frame, and first estimate a moduli potential by averaging localized sources. The 'abc' structure is U=Md^d η²[a−bη^((d−2)/2)+cη^(d−2)]; the stated positive-energy window is 1<4ac/b²<(d+2)²/(8d), evaluated after stabilizing the other moduli.

Quantize core–halo configurations using a graded Fock space built from reduced vanilla BPS states and electromagnetic angular momentum j=(|⟨γ_c,γ_h⟩|−1)/2; package their contributions using quantum dilogarithms.
For A1 theories, use WKB triangulations, flips implementing simple-root mutations, and the traffic-rule algorithm for framed indices. Irregular flat connections additionally require Stokes data.

Use M/F-theory duality and resolved Coulomb branches: exceptional divisors encode Dynkin intersections and harmonic two-forms supply vectors. The stated brane-vector count is n_v=h^(1,1)(resolved Y_G)−h^(1,1)(B)−1; subtract rank(G) for extra abelian factors.

Apply Tate's algorithm to the restricted model's curve C={b̃2=b̃3=0}; resolve it by introducing s and replacing x̃→x̃s, ỹ→ỹs. Toric mirror constructions and coefficient-monomial counts provide a complementary gauge-group diagnostic.

Express the mode evolution operator through Bogoliubov coefficients, evaluate its normalized trace over the initial thermal ensemble, and represent the same quantity as a thermofield-vacuum expectation value using a fictitious noninteracting copy.

Expand thermal corrections in Fermi-Dirac or Bose-Einstein factors and a complex parameter derived from μ. For the constant field, use the asymptotic longitudinal-state factor qE/(2π); the real-part expansion employs Bernoulli numbers and confluent hypergeometric functions.

Compare the four-form factor Y4 of the anomaly polynomial with dH3, where supersymmetry and gauge invariance require Chern–Simons modifications of the B2 field strength. The paper identifies their agreement as essential to Green–Schwarz cancellation.
Use the formal twelve-form anomaly polynomial and descent relations I12=dI11 and δI11=dI10 to relate its factorization to the anomalous variation of the quantum effective action.

Track the abelian variation of the Green–Schwarz counterterm and interpret the mismatch diagrammatically: tree-level B exchange generates contributions involving abelian gauge fields without corresponding one-loop hexagon anomalies.

G-structure reduction and representation theory organize differential constraints. For SU(3), dω and dΩ decompose into five intrinsic torsion classes W1,…,W5, distinguishing complex, symplectic, Kähler and Calabi–Yau cases.

The review uses contraction-plus-wedge Clifford action, Mukai pairings, the Courant bracket as a derived bracket, Clifford/Fierz maps to bispinors, and Hitchin's quartic construction. In six dimensions, q(ρ)<0 determines a nondegenerate complex pure spinor from its real part, up to conjugation.

Diagonalize volume expressions, normalize the inflaton using the Kähler metric, and approximate the e-fold integral and potential slow-roll parameters. Translate these into ns, αs and r and compare their ranges with the quoted WMAP7 data.

Apply the reviewed large-volume F-term construction using the corrected Kähler potential and nonperturbative superpotential. Examine stabilization through derivatives of the potential, loop corrections, D-terms and Kähler-cone restrictions in the concrete geometries.

The authors vary the bulk, boundary and shell actions to obtain scalar boundary conditions and modified Lanczos junction conditions. Constant bulk Φ removes the normal-derivative terms in the specialized shell equation.

They square the radial junction equation twice to obtain two effective-potential branches, inspect parameter examples, and recover normal orientations using effective extrinsic curvatures β±. Those orientations determine the causal embeddings; the potential alone does not.

Variation with respect to the spatial metric gives a second FRW equation. Matter conservation allows its integration to a first FRW equation with an integration term C/a³; projectability supplies a global lapse constraint.

An auxiliary scalar and a conformal transformation of the spatial metric expose a scalar potential and mass used to estimate fifth-force suppression. Future singularities are investigated separately through dominant behavior near H=h0/(ts−t)^q.

Reconstruction uses η=ln(a/a0) and G(η)=H², then expresses η through R̃ to obtain an ODE for F. The ΛCDM example becomes a hypergeometric equation; the matter-free phantom example becomes an Euler equation.

A flow method locates the apparent horizon. Its area, embedding shape, areal radius, and normalized curvature invariants constructed from Riemann contractions are monitored. Convergence tests supply error estimates where available.

Berger–Oliger adaptive mesh refinement uses refinement ratio two and truncation-error estimates. Three resolutions use tolerances τ0, τ0/8, and τ0/64; hierarchies eventually reach as many as 17 refinement levels.

The solver uses generalized harmonic evolution in Cartesian harmonic gauge, SO(3) reduction through a cartoon method, constraint damping with κ=1 and ρ=−0.5, fourth-order finite differences, and fourth-order Runge–Kutta time integration.

Solve early-time Friedmann evolution perturbatively in gravity, use numerical evolution and late-time asymptotic ansätze, and analyze linear homogeneous perturbations in regimes where their energy either dominates or perturbs the background energy.

Determine spectra through action symmetries and explicit modes; use Bogoliubov matching to radiation-era modes to quantify squeezing. Test superluminality using the fluctuation effective metric and the phase shift resolvable below an EFT cutoff.

Use ADM variables in unitary gauge, solve lapse and shift constraints and obtain Sζ=∫d⁴x a³[Aζ̇²−B(∇ζ)²/a²]. Newtonian gauge and Bardeen potentials identify the physical adiabatic modes and clarify the gravity-decoupling limit.

The equations are split into external and internal components. Factorized gaugino spinors obey a massless external Dirac equation, and assumed quantum averages of external bilinears supply a condensate source for the bosonic equations.

SU(3)-structure spinors, Killing-spinor identities, Fierz identities, and coset Maurer–Cartan equations determine flux and curvature contractions. A family of metric connections with skew torsion is examined, including the canonical and plus connections.

Lemma 4.1 relates an instanton's topological and norm expressions: if ∗F=−ω∧F and tr(F∧F)=(κ/ρ)dH, then tr|F|²=−κ/ρ² in the stated normalization. When both F and R̃ are instantons, this makes the relevant Bianchi and field-equation conditions equivalent.

Excursion curves and parameter trends are compared with parameter regions attributed to reference [31]. This is theoretical screening using previously supplied observational constraints; the paper does not present a new observational likelihood analysis.

The author numerically solves coupled redshift evolution equations for ΩD and H/H0, specifying present matter and curvature fractions and constants b,d. The resulting histories enter the excursion quadrature |Δφ(z)|/Mp=∫₀ᶻ√(3[1+wφ(z′)]Ωφ(z′)) dz′/(1+z′).

Stabilize the volume modulus numerically at general radius, integrate the radial kinetic coefficient to define canonical φ, and evaluate slow-roll e-folds and spectra. For large angular displacements, introduce χ1, χ2 and ξ and derive the potential and kinetic cross terms.

Use SU(2) Euler–Rodriguez coordinates, linear expansions to locate angular extrema, and quadratic expansions to diagonalize their Hessian. The resulting eigenvalues are XP, XQ, XQ, XR, XR; relations to Cayley–Kline coordinates supply the kinetic metric.

Construct the N=1 supergravity F-term potential using W=W0+A(z)e^(−aρ), A=A0[f(z)/f(0)]^(1/n), and κ²K=−3 log(ρ+ρ̄−γk). The calculation uses the deformed-conifold metric rather than directly solving the ten-dimensional Φ− equation.

Flux quantization is inverted using B-shift-invariant integer combinations, including n2²−2n0n4 and n2³+3n0²n6−3n0n2n4. For N=2, pure-spinor supersymmetry equations reduce to three first-order ODEs; pole expansions and numerical matching determine the regular symmetric family.

A timelike-frame component of the string-frame Einstein equation expresses a two-derivative NS–NS combination, multiplied by e^(−2φ), as a sum of nonnegative electric and magnetic RR-flux squares. Quantization supplies a nonzero lower scale through F0.

Monopoles are analyzed by radial quantization on R×S², classical BPS matter constraints, Chern–Simons-induced electric charges, and a one-loop Casimir-energy contribution. Wrapped-brane probes are subjected to BPS, world-volume flux quantization, and tadpole-cancellation conditions.

Numerically solve the homogeneous scalar and Friedmann equations using Mathematica with data imposed at the bounce. The example uses α=4, M=2×10^(−3), V=1/(φ⁴+10¹²), and ρm(0)=10^(−12), in the stated Planck units; it demonstrates a chosen solution rather than generic initial-condition selection.

Expand φ=ct+π and derive homogeneous energy, pressure and scalar evolution to leading order in π̇/c. Compare ghost-energy growth with a power-law contracting background and with matter, radiation and anisotropy scalings.

Split the Newtonian potential into matter and ghost-induced parts. Solve the long-wavelength sourced equation with Green functions, treat the k⁴ correction by a Born approximation, and estimate bounce evolution through an oscillator equation and an instability growth-rate bound.

Relate scalar charges to derivatives of atomic masses by the chain rule. QCD trace-anomaly and renormalization-group arguments give RG-invariant definitions of d_g and the quark-mass couplings; electromagnetic running is neglected.

Combine a semi-empirical nuclear mass formula with scalar/vector contact-interaction descriptions of nuclear binding and imported chiral/dispersive estimates of two-pion exchange. Infer quark-mass sensitivity through m_π²≈b₀Λ₃m̂, including induced changes in density, asymmetry energy and Coulomb energy.

Dimensionally reduce the supersymmetry-fixed ten-dimensional action on the α′-corrected background through O(α′²), retaining two spacetime derivatives. Work initially in string frame, then perform a Weyl transformation and dualize the spacetime B field to obtain the Einstein-frame action.

Reconstruct K from the real Kähler-modulus kinetic metric using axion shifts. Expand the corrected fundamental form and use harmonic orthogonality, Ricci flatness and integrated total derivatives to identify cancellations and the surviving norm-squared term.

Determine the first metric correction h from a gauge-fixed Lichnerowicz equation sourced by gauge-curvature and Riemann-curvature bilinears. Absorb homogeneous zero modes into moduli redefinitions and select corrections orthogonal to harmonic modes.

Closed-string amplitudes are obtained through KLT from α′-expanded ordered open-string amplitudes. Supersymmetry Ward identities supply missing six-point NMHV components from a five-amplitude basis; the authors automate this construction in Mathematica using supplied open-string amplitude code.

Local operator superamplitudes are constructed from spinor-helicity polynomials constrained by mass dimension, little-group scaling, supersymmetry Ward identities, and permutation symmetry. Super-KLT classifies reduced-symmetry sectors by two integers, N^(k,k̃)MHV, inherited from the two open-string factors.

Two methods isolate the SU(8) singlet: averaging over 35 scalar-index arrangements, with weights 1/35, −16/35, and 18/35 for the three canonical scalar classes; and explicitly subtracting the local SU(8)-violating six-point superamplitude. The minus sign in the averaging is essential.
Cosmological evolution is recast as motion in a one-dimensional scale-factor potential. A separate free-scalar implementation uses exact UV mode functions rather than only a WKB approximation.

Weighted power counting under t→b^z t and x→bx gives scalar scaling dimension s=(3−z)/2. At z=3, sixth spatial derivatives balance the second time derivatives; this motivates the gravitational operator construction.

The scalar sector is examined by solving momentum constraints in a metric perturbation expansion, then replacing that expansion with nonlinear radial equations for static spherical vacuum configurations and selecting a particular solution branch.

Study integration of infinitesimal lifts through a central extension 1→U(1)→G̃→G→1, and compare lifts using Čech transition functions and connections. GIT examples use Proj of graded invariant sections to relate linearization weights to quotient Kähler classes.

Identify moment-map translations with changes in fermionic gauge transformations through F^(a)=X^(a)K+iD^(a). Equivariance of D ensures that the resulting infinitesimal transformations obey the Lie algebra.

Expand to quadratic order in unitary-gauge perturbations and eliminate lapse and shift through their constraints. Use dy=c_s dτ and a canonically normalized mode to obtain a Sasaki–Mukhanov-type equation, then evaluate the spectrum with Hankel modes.

Vary the action to obtain the stress tensor and background equations, then solve the shift-symmetric de Sitter conditions. Numerical integrations examine quasi-de Sitter attraction and an exit produced by changing the sign of the linear kinetic coefficient.

Monopole screening identifies Wilson lines; ribbon fusion and Aharonov–Bohm transport determine associators and braidings. Pentagon, hexagon, and boundary hexagon relations organize the resulting categorical consistency conditions.

Boundary calculations use BRST gauge fixing in Lorenz gauge, a splitting of the boundary charge sequence, and the method of image charges. Final boundary associators and semi-braidings are expressed independently of the splitting, up to the stated equivalences.

The folding trick converts surface defects to boundaries of a theory with K⊕(−K). Interval reduction gives a two-dimensional BF-type theory. Stable lattice equivalence and an explicit invertible wall for the hyperbolic lattice U support the quantum classification.

Use bosonic and fermionic Gibbons–Hawking–York terms, supersymmetry orbits of modified boundary conditions, Israel junction conditions and Noether coupling to match boundary actions with bulk surface variations.
Match polynomial coefficients between classical and quantum anomalies. The paper supplies a numerical real-parameter solution and notes that Gröbner bases simplify the simultaneous equations.

Compute one-loop eight-form anomaly polynomials and classical descent anomalies, add local counterterms to obtain consistent anomalies, and use boundary tensor terms B₂ˣ∧G₄ᵃ for generalized Green–Schwarz cancellation.
Generalized Green–Schwarz–Sagnotti factorization writes I8=(1/2)ΩαβX4αX4β. Anomaly equations determine inner products of a and bi, including a²=9−T and the gravitational condition H−V=273−29T.

The integrality argument uses Young-tableau trace congruences for classical groups and branching through maximal subgroups for other groups. SU(2), SU(3) and G2 require the additional global-anomaly conditions; local anomaly cancellation alone is insufficient for these factors.

The finiteness proof proceeds by contradiction, separating unbounded numbers of bounded-size simple factors from unbounded-size factors. It combines Lorentzian inner-product geometry, hypermultiplet counting, Turán’s graph theorem and restrictions on large-rank representations.

Constrained chiral spinors are represented as vector-multiplet field strengths of real prepotentials V and U. Improvement transformations are then used to test equivalence with the Ferrara–Zumino multiplet, subject to global well-definedness.

For theories with a known off-shell supergravity coupling, the author also describes obtaining a rigid current by varying the curved-space action with respect to supergravity prepotentials and then switching off the gravitational background.

The superfield Noether calculation promotes a super-Poincaré variation to δΦ^I=−¼D̄²(L^αD_αΦ^I), with arbitrary spinor superfield L^α. The coefficient of L^α in the action variation gives the supercurrent conservation law upon imposing the matter equations of motion.
The theoretical selection is Δφ(zm)/Mp=∫₀^zm sqrt(3|(1+w(z))Ωφ(z)|) dz/(1+z)<1. The paper integrates the model evolution and evaluates this condition, normally taking zm=1090.

The dark-energy fraction is evolved using dΩφ/dz=[3wΩφ(1−Ωφ)−κ²Q/(3H³)]/(1+z). Substituting each coupling and equation of state yields the background equations used for the excursion calculation and distance predictions.

Historical observational fits minimize a combined χ² using Union2’s 557 supernovae with systematic covariance, SDSS BAO distance ratios and the WMAP5 CMB shift parameter. Constitution’s 397 supernovae provide a systematic comparison. Luminosity, angular and dilation distances are computed from E(z)=H/H0.

Voigt-profile fitting with vpfit minimizes χ² simultaneously across species. Related redshifts and broadening parameters are tied; thermal and turbulent limiting models are likelihood-weighted. Velocity structure is finalized before introducing Δα/α as a free parameter; isotopic and hyperfine structure are included where available and appropriate.

The Many Multiplet method compares relative transition wavenumbers with laboratory values. Transition sensitivities Q differ in magnitude and sign, which the authors use to distinguish an α shift from some systematic shifts. The extracted wavenumber equation is garbled and is not reconstructed here.

An empirical additional-error term is estimated using a monopole fit and modified Least Trimmed Squares retaining the 85% smallest squared residuals. Dipole significance is assessed by randomizing associations between Δα/α and sightline/redshift, refitting, and comparing χ² distributions.

Integration by parts, classical SM equations of motion, derivative commutators proportional to field strengths, and Bianchi identities reduce derivative-rich classes to lower classes. The on-shell irrelevance of EOM-redundant operators, including the cited all-orders and nonperturbative statement, is imported background.

Operators are enumerated from matter fields, field strengths and covariant derivatives using canonical dimensions, Lorentz contractions, hypercharge and gauge-representation constraints. A simple computer-algebra search tests zero-hypercharge four-fermion field contents before singlet contractions are classified.

Fierz identities for anticommuting fermion fields, together with Pauli-matrix and SU(3) generator identities, remove redundant four-fermion contractions. The reductions must retain all possible flavor assignments; generation permutations are part of the identities.

Dimensional reduction over the magnetized S² produces a four-dimensional canonical radion ψ and effective potential. Its extrema distinguish stable compactifications from unstable branches that can roll toward another extremum or decompactification.

For de Sitter solutions, the fields are analytically continued across the cosmological horizon to ds²=−dt²+B²(t)dH3²+C²(t)dΩ2². Numerical future evolution determines whether the solution approaches a four-dimensional flux vacuum or decompactifies toward dS6.

A hedgehog Higgs/gauge ansatz and warped metric reduce the construction to coupled ordinary differential equations with regular-core and compactification boundary conditions. Multiple shooting divides the interval into short segments and uses Newton matching to avoid exponentially growing numerical modes.

The finiteness argument proceeds by contradiction, separating unbounded numbers of bounded-size simple factors from factors of unbounded dimension. It combines Lorentzian lattice geometry, classification by the sign of b_i², Turán’s theorem and large-rank representation constraints.

Review of index-theoretic anomaly polynomials and Green–Schwarz–Sagnotti factorization I8=(1/2)ΩαβX4αX4β. Group-theoretic trace coefficients constrain matter multiplicities and anomaly-vector inner products, including H−V=273−29T and a²=9−T.

The geometric analysis maps anomaly data to intersection data on B and tests lattice embeddings, effectiveness and the Kodaira discriminant relation. Actual realization additionally requires a Weierstrass model with the desired singularities.

Construct localised solutions by adding a warp factor, a sourced RR component and a varying dilaton. The remaining equations reduce to relations among these fields and a Poisson equation with flux and delta-function source terms.

Work directly with ten-dimensional Einstein, dilaton, flux equations and Bianchi identities. Combining the traced external Einstein equation, dilaton equation and sourced Bianchi identity gives a Laplacian identity with nonnegative squares; compact integration constrains curvature and forces BPS relations at Minkowski points.

Apply double dimensional reduction with y=ξ², xμ=zμ(ξ⁰,ξ¹), and y-independent metric and contortion. Decompose the metric into gμν, aμ and φ, and the axial contortion into lower-dimensional two-form and three-form components.
